title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. The study developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV.
analysis.methods: The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions.
analysis.main_results: Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 10^1 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool for HFRS.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. However, no negative samples were included, so negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop a rapid diagnostic assay for the dual detection of Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV), which are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection, using virus-specific sgRNAs and primers targeting conserved genomic regions. The results showed that both HTNV and SEOV could be detected at a threshold of 1 × 10^1 copies/test in three technical replicates, indicating the assay's high sensitivity. However, the study did not include negative samples, limiting the ability to assess specificity and false-positive rates. The findings suggest that the assay has potential as a screening tool for HFRS but require validation with larger studies using well-characterized clinical specimens. The study's results are limited by the absence of negative controls, which affects the strength of the evidence for diagnostic accuracy.

title: An ONT sequencing framework for hantavirus genome assembly, variant analysis, and defective viral genome characterization from whole-segment amplicons

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses that can cause severe human disease, necessitating improved methods for genome assembly and variant analysis.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces an Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing framework tailored for hantavirus genome assembly and variant analysis. The framework utilizes universal reverse transcription primers and species-specific primer pairs to amplify and sequence complete S, M, and L segments, along with a bioinformatic pipeline for reference-guided assembly and DVG classification. Applied to diverse hantavirus strains, including Puumala virus, Old World, and New World orthohantaviruses, the method accurately reconstructed full genomes and identified abundant defective viral genomes (DVGs) and conserved L segment deletions. These findings reveal DVGs as a previously unrecognized feature of hantavirus populations, offering a low-cost, adaptable workflow for hantavirus genomics. The study highlights the limitations of existing methods in capturing viral heterogeneity but demonstrates the effectiveness of its approach in reconstructing genomes, providing moderate confidence in its utility for surveillance and understanding viral evolution.

analysis.methods: Lung tissue samples from 329 animals collected in September were examined in 123 pooled testing units, whereas 14 animals collected in July were tested individually. Real-time and conventional RT-PCR were used to evaluate 137 testing units representing 343 animals. The minimum infection rate (MIR) was calculated as a descriptive estimate, and a pooled-testing likelihood model was used to account for variation in testing-unit size.

Positive testing units were observed among the Ural field mouse (Apodemus uralensis), bank vole (Myodes glareolus), and common vole (Microtus arvalis).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found a significant presence of hantavirus RNA in small mammals, with a higher infection rate than previously reported. analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational nature and the use of pooled testing, which may underestimate the true infection rate. title: Expanded protocadherin-1 usage reveals a broader hantavirus entry landscape

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the cellular entry mechanisms of hantaviruses, as the entry mechanisms of most hantaviruses remain poorly defined. Mammalian hantaviruses are RNA viruses that cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system to examine entry by phylogenetically distinct hantaviruses identified across Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas. The rVSVs were generated bearing Gn/Gc proteins from Necoclí, Sangassou, Thottapalayam, Kenkeme, Nova, Oxbow, and Tula viruses.
analysis.methods: Using a BSL2-compatible recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) system, the researchers generated replication-competent rVSVs bearing Gn/Gc proteins from various hantaviruses and tested their ability to mediate infection of primary human endothelial cells.
analysis.main_results: Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. All these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells, broaden the phylogenetic scope of PCDH1-dependent entry, and identify receptor-targeted and viral glycoprotein-targeted strategies with differential activity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the receptor usage of hantaviruses, which can inform the development of targeted therapies and improve understanding of the mechanisms underlying hantavirus infection and disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study used a surrogate system and an authentic Tula virus experiment to support its conclusions, which provides moderate confidence in the findings. The antibody neutralization results suggest variability in the effectiveness of broadly reactive countermeasures.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the cellular entry mechanisms of hantaviruses, focusing on the ability of different hantavirus glycoproteins to mediate infection of human endothelial cells. The researchers generated replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing Gn/Gc proteins from various hantaviruses and tested their infectivity. They found that all these Gn/Gc proteins except Kenkeme supported infection of primary human endothelial cells, indicating that endothelial cell entry is permissive for a broader range of hantaviruses than previously thought. Genetic studies in human cells lacking protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) showed that Necoclí, Tula, and Nova viruses use PCDH1 for efficient infection, although the Nova phenotype was weaker. The findings expand the range of hantavirus glycoproteins capable of mediating infection of human endothelial cells and highlight the potential and limitations of broadly reactive anti-Gn/Gc antibodies as countermeasures. The study provides moderate confidence in its conclusions, supported by both a surrogate system and an authentic Tula virus experiment.

The review also notes that thrombotic, hemorrhagic, and leaky phenotypes are interconnected outcomes influenced by viral tropism, immune activation, and host factors. The analysis underscores the need for further research into these vascular mechanisms to improve diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available.
analysis.study_design_and_population: New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1.
analysis.methods: However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear.
analysis.main_results: Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the structural basis of PCDH1 recognition by New World hantaviruses, specifically Andes virus (ANDV). The research addresses the lack of approved therapeutics for hantavirus infections, which are severe and rodent-borne. The study describes the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution, revealing how the receptor asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers. This explains the requirement for intact viral particles or soluble tetramers to recognize PCDH1. The findings also show that neutralizing antibodies block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms, providing insights into antiviral therapeutic design. The study contributes to understanding hantavirus-receptor interactions and highlights potential strategies for targeting the viral spike. However, the evidence is limited to structural and functional analyses of ANDV, and the findings are specific to this virus.

title: Biocontainment Transport of Patients with High-Consequence Infectious Diseases: A Narrative Review and Integrated Operational Framework for Emergency Medical Systems

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on the transport of patients with high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs), particularly those caused by hantaviruses, and aims to develop an integrated operational framework for emergency medical systems. The central question is how to safely move patients with hantavirus infections between different care settings while maintaining biosafety.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review conducted a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus up to 10 October 2026, incorporating guidance from the World Health Organization, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and national authorities. The findings were reported according to the SANRA scale and organized across seven operational domains, combined with the operational experience of the Italian Red Cross biocontainment transport service.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The literature is dominated by aeromedical case reports, technical evaluations, and expert consensus, with few comparative studies. Recurrent findings include device integrity and air quality within transport isolators, the risk of self-contamination during doffing, heat strain, communication limits imposed by personal protective equipment, decontamination of vehicles and isolators, team readiness during low-activity periods, and the psychological burden on patients and staff. These findings are integrated into a framework comprising a four-link containment chain, a seven-phase operational workflow, a three-tier complexity classification, and a role-based responsibility matrix.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The literature lacks comparative studies, and the findings are primarily based on case reports and technical evaluations. There is limited evidence on the effectiveness of specific interventions, and the framework components require prospective evaluation. Additionally, the review notes that the operational experience of the Italian Red Cross biocontainment transport service is a key source of data, but this may not be representative of all emergency medical systems.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The framework proposed in the review is a structured, consensus-based reference for planning, training, and quality assurance in biocontainment transport. It highlights the need for prospective evaluation of its components and emphasizes the importance of integrating operational experience into the development of emergency medical systems. The review also underscores the necessity for further research on the effectiveness of interventions and the development of standardized protocols for biocontainment transport.

analysis.summary_en: This narrative review addresses the transport of patients with hantavirus infections, focusing on the integration of biosafety science and emergency medicine. It synthesizes the international literature on biocontainment transport and develops an operational framework for emergency medical systems. The review highlights recurrent findings such as device integrity, air quality, self-contamination risks, heat strain, communication challenges, and psychological burdens. It emphasizes the need for a structured, consensus-based approach and calls for prospective evaluation of the framework components. The review also identifies gaps in comparative studies and underscores the importance of operational experience in shaping best practices for biocontainment transport.
